Vignette:
A 56-year-old woman who is a long-time patient returns to the office for scheduled follow up of her type 2 diabetes and chronically elevated blood glucose. At her last visit 3 months ago, her HbA1C was 7.6%, where it had been for several visits. You recommended beginning treatment with insulin, which she refused because of her fear of needles. You then increased her dose of glimepiride from 4 mg to 8 mg once a day and advised her to more strictly follow her diet and exercise regimen, which she claims to be doing. Since the last visit, her home fingerstick glucose levels have ranged from 119 mg/dL to 263 mg/dL (6.6 to 14.6 mmol/L) and her weight on her home scale is unchanged at about 98 kg. She describes increased thirst and urination but denies blurry vision, nonhealing ulcers, or lethargy.

Per office protocol, a fingerstick glucose test on arrival today shows glucose level of 221mg/dL (12.27 mmol/L) and hemoglobin A1C 8.1%; urine dipstick is normal.

Review of Systems:
General: Increased thirst and is drinking more water. Appetite is normal and her weight at home has been unchanged for several months. She denies lethargy, fever, chills, or night sweats.

Skin: No rash, pruritus, or lesions

HEENT: No change in vision, sore throat, dysphagia

Pulmonary: No cough, shortness of breath, wheezing

Cardiovascular: No chest pain, pressure, or discomfort; no orthopnea, dyspnea on exertion, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea

Genitourinary: Increased urinary frequency without urgency, dysuria, or blood in urine. No vaginal discharge or itching.

Musculoskeletal: No joint or muscle pain, no sores or lesions on feet.

Neurologic: Has numbness and tingling in both feet that comes and goes throughout the day. No headache, tremor, change in gait.

Psychiatric: No mood swings, depression, or anxiety.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and obesity

Surgical history: Cholecystectomy 5 years prior

Medications: Metformin 1000 mg twice a day, atorvastatin 80 mg once a day, glimepiride 8 mg once a day with breakfast, lisinopril 40 mg once a day, all of which she claims to be taking faithfully.

Allergies: Penicillin, which causes rash

Family history: Father died from myocardial infarction at age 89 years, mother age 88 years has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

Social history: Patient works as a social worker, has never smoked cigarettes, denies any illicit drug use, drinks 1 to 2 glasses of wine with dinner every night. She rides a stationary bike about 1 to 2 days per week for 20 minutes, which she has been able to do without difficulty. She is up to date with all immunizations. Her diet consists mainly of pizza, chicken, vegetables, fruit, pasta, and diet sodas. She is married and has a 12-year-old son. She is intermittently sexually active with her husband 1 to 2 times per month. They do not use contraception as she is no longer menstruating.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Well-appearing female in no apparent distress, height 1.65 m, weight 95.3 kg (BMI 34.9)

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 82 min
BP: 159/88 mmHg
Respirations: 12/min

Skin: There is velvety smooth hyperpigmentation in neck folds and under arms; no other lesions or rash.

HEENT: Moist mucous membranes, no exudates, no cervical lymphadenopathy.

Pulmonary: Clear to auscultation bilaterally, no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Jugular venous distention normal.

Gastrointestinal: Obese abdomen, soft, non-distended, normal bowel sounds, no rebound or guarding.

Genitourinary: No signs of yeast infection or other lesions. No tenderness to flank percussion.

Musculoskeletal: No peripheral edema, swelling or tenderness. Joints full range of motion and nontender.

Neurologic: Decreased sensation to light touch in feet bilaterally. Cranial nerves II to VIII grossly intact, normal gait, strength 5/5 throughout.

Mental status: Alert and oriented x3

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and are shown:

Serum

HbA1C: 8.1%
Glucose: 221 mg/dL (12.27 mmol/L)
Sodium: 138 mEq/L (138 mmol/L)
Potassium: 4.1 mEq/L (4.1 mmol/L)
Creatinine: 0.7 mg/dL ( 62 µmol/L)
BUN: 23 mg/dL (8.2 mmol/L)
Lipid Panel: Results pending
winner_protocol:
Age: 56 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Follow-up of type 2 diabetes mellitus with worsening hyperglycemia (HbA1C 8.1%), increased thirst and urinary frequency, and symptoms of peripheral neuropathy despite treatment with metformin and glimepiride.
Analysis: The patient demonstrates inadequate glycemic control, with an HbA1C of 8.1% and an office glucose of 221 mg/dL while on metformin 1000 mg twice daily and glimepiride 8 mg daily. Supporting facts include home glucose readings up to 263 mg/dL, obesity (BMI 34.9), physical findings of acanthosis nigricans, and decreased sensation to light touch in the feet with intermittent numbness and tingling consistent with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. She is hemodynamically stable and well-appearing without signs of diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar crisis. Main relevant differential considerations center on the etiology of her urinary symptoms: osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia is most likely, whereas a urinary tract infection is less supported given the normal urine dipstick and absence of dysuria or urgency. For her neuropathy, the primary consideration is diabetic peripheral neuropathy, though metformin-associated vitamin B12 deficiency remains a possibility to exclude.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; formal diabetic foot examination with 10-g monofilament and vibration testing; dilated funduscopic examination by ophthalmology; serum vitamin B12 level.
Conclusion: A 56-year-old woman with obesity and long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with progressive, symptomatic hyperglycemia (HbA1C 8.1%) despite dual oral therapy, with physical findings of insulin resistance and early diabetic peripheral neuropathy. She remains hypertensive and currently declines insulin.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: 1) Intensify glycemic control by adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist (e.g., oral semaglutide or a once-weekly injectable formulation) or an SGLT2 inhibitor; given her obesity and insulin resistance, a GLP-1 RA is preferred for glycemic efficacy and weight benefit. If hypoglycemia becomes a concern with combination therapy, consider reducing glimepiride. 2) Optimize blood pressure, as her BP of 159/88 is above goal; add a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic to lisinopril and reinforce sodium restriction. 3) Continue metformin; reassess the need for glimepiride if adding agents with lower hypoglycemia risk. 4) Obtain a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio to screen for diabetic kidney disease. 5) Arrange formal foot neuropathy assessment and counsel on daily foot inspections given decreased sensation. 6) Arrange a dilated eye examination if not performed within the past year. 7) Check a serum vitamin B12 level given metformin use and neuropathy. 8) When the pending lipid panel returns, verify statin adequacy; she is already on high-intensity atorvastatin. 9) Revisit insulin need and address her fear of needles with education about modern pen needles; if refusal persists, maximize non-insulin options and set clear glycemic targets for future insulin initiation. 10) Refer to diabetes education and medical nutrition therapy to improve dietary choices and increase physical activity beyond the current 1-2 days per week.
Notes: Alcohol consumption in combination with glimepiride may increase hypoglycemia risk and should be reviewed.

Diagnosis10cm: Left tubal pregnancy without intrauterine pregnancy
Vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness that began 45 minutes ago. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate 2 years ago. On examination, she is pale, diaphoretic, and appears acutely ill. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 78/48, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with peritoneal signs. Pelvic exam demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and a tender left adnexal mass. Quantitative beta-hCG is 4,200 mIU/mL. Bedside transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a complex left adnexal mass with ring-of-fire sign, and significant free fluid in the pelvis and Morison's pouch. Hemoglobin returns at 7.8 g/dL. O-negative blood is ordered and the OR is alerted for emergent laparotomy.

tags: ['axis:accuracy']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[2]
tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

[3]
tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[4]
tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

[5]
tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe left-sided pelvic pain and lightheadedness that began 45 minutes ago. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhea and a positive home pregnancy test 5 days ago. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease and a prior left tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate 2 years ago. On examination, she is pale, diaphoretic, and appears acutely ill. Pelvic exam demonstrates cervical motion tenderness and a tender left adnexal mass. Quantitative beta-hCG is 4,200 mIU/mL. A 35-year-old man who jogs regularly presents with a 1-week history of an itchy rash in his groin folds. He reports the itch worsens after running and sweating. He denies any genital lesions, urinary symptoms, or prior similar episodes. On examination, there are bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with slightly raised scaly borders along the inguinal creases extending to the proximal inner thighs. The scrotum is spared. winner_protocol:
Age: 35-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: 1-week history of an itchy rash in the groin folds that worsens after running and sweating.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with tinea cruris. Key supporting features include bilateral, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with slightly raised scaly borders localized to the inguinal creases and proximal inner thighs; exacerbation with heat and moisture from running and sweating; and sparing of the scrotum with absence of satellite lesions. These findings favor a dermatophyte infection over candidal intertrigo, which typically involves the scrotum and demonstrates satellite pustules. Erythrasma is a consideration but usually presents with less active scale and would show coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp. Inverse psoriasis is possible but less likely without a history of psoriasis or involvement of other intertriginous areas. Contact or irritant dermatitis is less consistent with the well-demarcated scaly advancing border. No central clearing does not exclude tinea cruris.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: KOH preparation of skin scrapings from the active scaly border to identify fungal hyphae.
Conclusion: Tinea cruris (dermatophyte infection of the groin).
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: 1. Perform a KOH preparation of skin scrapings from the active border to confirm dermatophyte infection. 2. Initiate topical antifungal therapy applied to the affected area and a 2 cm margin beyond the visible lesion, typically twice daily for 1 to 2 weeks (allylamines) or 2 to 4 weeks (azoles), continuing for at least one week after clinical clearing. 3. Counsel on moisture control: dry the groin thoroughly after bathing and exercise, change out of sweaty clothing promptly, and wear loose, breathable fabrics to reduce maceration. 4. Assess for concurrent tinea pedis, which may serve as a reservoir for reinfection, and treat if identified. 5. Avoid topical corticosteroid monotherapy, as it can mask the infection and lead to tinea incognito. 6. If KOH is negative or there is no response to appropriate antifungal therapy, reconsider alternative diagnoses such as inverse psoriasis, erythrasma, or contact dermatitis.
Notes: Scrotal sparing and the absence of satellite lesions are important clinical clues that distinguish tinea cruris from candidal intertrigo. Bilateral inguinal involvement does not exclude a dermatophyte infection.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

Vignette:
A 22-year-old female soccer player presents to the sports medicine clinic two days after sustaining a left knee injury during a game. She reports that while pivoting to change direction she felt a sudden pop in her knee followed by immediate swelling and inability to continue playing. She was unable to bear full weight and has been using crutches since. She denies any prior knee injuries. On examination, there is a moderate effusion of the left knee. Range of motion is limited by pain and swelling. The Lachman test is positive with a soft endpoint on the left, and the anterior drawer test demonstrates increased anterior tibial translation compared to the right. McMurray test is equivocal. The collateral ligaments are stable. She is neurovascularly intact distally.
winner_protocol:
Age: 22-year-old
Sex: Female
Complaint: Acute left knee pain, swelling, and instability following a pivoting injury sustained during a soccer game two days prior.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for an acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. The strongest supporting facts are the pivoting mechanism, reported audible pop, immediate swelling consistent with hemarthrosis, positive Lachman test with a soft endpoint, and increased anterior tibial translation on anterior drawer testing. The stable collateral ligaments and intact distal neurovascular status argue against a multi-ligamentous knee dislocation or vascular injury. The main differential considerations include a concurrent meniscal tear (the McMurray test is equivocal and meniscal pathology frequently coexists with ACL injury), tibial spine avulsion fracture, and patellar dislocation, though the latter two are less consistent with the ligamentous examination findings.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Knee radiographs (anteroposterior and lateral) to exclude fracture or avulsion; MRI of the left knee to confirm ACL integrity and evaluate the menisci and articular cartilage.
Conclusion: Acute isolated left anterior cruciate ligament rupture with moderate intra-articular effusion/hemarthrosis in a young athlete.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Obtain knee radiographs and MRI. Continue protected weight-bearing with crutches and use a knee immobilizer or hinged brace. Implement RICE measures (rest, ice, compression, elevation) and analgesia as needed for pain and swelling. Arrange urgent referral to orthopedic or sports medicine specialist for definitive management. Avoid pivoting, cutting, jumping, or return to sport until cleared. Initiate gentle range-of-motion and quadriceps activation exercises as tolerated pending specialist evaluation if referral is delayed.
Notes: An equivocal McMurray test does not exclude an associated meniscal injury.

Vignette: A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician by his mother who noticed patches of hair loss on his scalp over the past 3 weeks. The patches have been gradually enlarging and the affected areas appear scaly. He attends elementary school and his mother reports several classmates have had similar issues. He denies pain but admits to mild itching. On examination, there are two well-defined round patches of alopecia on the parietal and occipital scalp, measuring approximately 3 cm and 2 cm in diameter respectively. Within the patches, the hair shafts are broken off at the surface giving a black-dot appearance. The surrounding scalp is covered with fine gray-white scale. There is mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. A Wood lamp examination reveals no fluorescence. KOH preparation of plucked hairs shows endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft.
winner_protocol:
Age: 6 years old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Patches of hair loss on the scalp with scaling and mild itching over the past 3 weeks.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for tinea capitis. The strongest supporting facts are: well-defined round patches of alopecia with black-dot broken hairs at the surface, fine gray-white scale on the surrounding scalp, mild posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, a history of similar issues among classmates suggesting contagious spread, negative Wood lamp examination, and KOH preparation demonstrating endothrix spores surrounding and within the hair shaft. The endothrix pattern and non-fluorescent Wood lamp examination are consistent with Trichophyton species. Relevant differential considerations include alopecia areata (typically lacks scale, broken hairs, and lymphadenopathy), trichotillomania (usually shows irregular patches and no scale), and seborrheic dermatitis (diffuse scaling without focal alopecia); however, the combination of black-dot alopecia, scaling, lymphadenopathy, contact history, and confirmatory KOH findings establishes tinea capitis definitively.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Tinea capitis (dermatophyte infection of the scalp), most consistent with an endothrix Trichophyton species, based on the clinical appearance of scaly, black-dot alopecic patches, reactive lymphadenopathy, negative Wood lamp fluorescence, and endothrix spores on KOH preparation.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Initiate systemic oral antifungal therapy, as topical agents alone do not adequately penetrate hair follicles for cure. Use an antifungal shampoo adjunctively to reduce spore shedding and contagiousness. Screen household members and close contacts for similar scalp lesions and treat them if present. Avoid sharing combs, hats, pillows, or hair accessories. Given the cluster of cases among classmates, consider notifying the school or relevant public health authorities. Arrange follow-up to assess clinical response and hair regrowth.
Notes: Topical antifungal monotherapy is insufficient for tinea capitis; oral systemic treatment is required to eradicate the dermatophyte within the hair shaft.

Vignette:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the ER after being stung by a bee at a picnic. He is crying hysterically. After 15 minutes of calming him down, exam reveals a swollen tender upper lip but no tongue swelling, no drooling, no stridor, no rash, and no other complaints.
winner_protocol:
Age: 9-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Bee sting with swollen, tender upper lip
Analysis: The patient presents with a localized reaction to a Hymenoptera sting confined to the upper lip. The strongest supporting facts are the witnessed bee sting, the localized swollen and tender lip, and the explicit absence of airway or systemic allergic signs—specifically no tongue swelling, drooling, stridor, rash, or other complaints. The hysterical crying resolved with calming, consistent with pain and distress rather than hypoxia or circulatory compromise. The primary differential is a large local cutaneous reaction versus early anaphylaxis; however, the lack of mucosal, respiratory, cutaneous, or gastrointestinal involvement makes isolated large local reaction the most likely diagnosis. Because the sting involves the face, there is an elevated risk for delayed progression involving deeper tissues or airway structures, necessitating close observation even though the current examination is reassuring.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Localized upper lip reaction following Hymenoptera envenomation without current evidence of anaphylaxis or airway compromise.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Maintain observation in the emergency department with serial reassessments of the airway, oropharynx, and vital signs to detect delayed anaphylaxis or progression of facial swelling. Apply cold compresses to the upper lip. Administer an oral antihistamine for localized swelling and pruritus, and provide analgesia for tenderness. Re-examine the oral cavity and sting site once the patient is calm to ensure no occult tongue or pharyngeal edema is developing. Discharge after an uneventful observation period with strict return precautions for tongue or throat swelling, voice changes, stridor, wheezing, difficulty breathing, widespread rash, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, or syncope. Counsel the family that facial Hymenoptera stings carry a higher risk of airway involvement and that future stings may trigger more severe reactions; advise follow-up with an allergist if any systemic symptoms occur.
Notes: Facial Hymenoptera envenomations warrant heightened vigilance for airway compromise despite an initially benign examination, and anaphylaxis can present with delayed onset.

Analysis: The clinical picture is classic for an acute thrombosed external hemorrhoid. The strongest supporting facts are the sudden onset during Valsalva maneuver (straining), the physical finding of a tense, bluish-purple, spherical, tender nodule at the anal verge, and the absence of infectious signs (no fever, erythema, or purulent drainage). The character of the pain—constant, throbbing, and severe—aligns with a perianal hematoma. Main relevant differential considerations include a perianal abscess (typically accompanied by erythema, warmth, fever, or purulent drainage, which are absent) and a strangulated or prolapsed internal hemorrhoid (usually presents as more proximal anal tissue rather than a discrete bluish nodule at the verge). Conclusion: Acute thrombosed external hemorrhoid in a 55-year-old male with occupational and dietary risk factors.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Initiate conservative measures including warm sitz baths several times daily, topical analgesics, and oral NSAIDs if not contraindicated. Begin bowel regimen optimization with a high-fiber diet, increased fluid intake, and a stool softener or osmotic laxative to minimize straining. Because symptoms began within the last 72 hours and pain is severe, arrange prompt evaluation by a general surgeon for consideration of office-based excision or thrombectomy. Address occupational risk factors by recommending periodic breaks from prolonged sitting and use of a cushioned surface while driving. Reassess urgently if fever, spreading erythema, purulent drainage, or changes in bowel habits develop.
Notes: Surgical excision/thrombectomy is generally most beneficial when performed within 48–72 hours of symptom onset; beyond this window, conservative management is usually preferred unless pain remains intolerable.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

A 22-year-old student presents with a 5-year history of worsening nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching. Symptoms are year-round but worse during the spring season. On further questioning it is revealed that he has significant eye itching, redness, and tearing as well as palate and throat itching during the spring season. winner_protocol:
Age: 22
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive nasal congestion, sneezing, and nasal itching over 5 years, with seasonal worsening in spring and associated ocular itching/redness/tearing as well as palate and throat itching.
Analysis: The patient’s pattern of nasal and ocular pruritus, sneezing, and congestion with a clear springtime exacerbation is highly consistent with IgE-mediated allergic rhinitis with allergic conjunctivitis. Supporting features include multi-organ involvement (nasal, conjunctival, and oropharyngeal itching), a temporal relationship to spring (suggesting pollens), and a personal history of infantile eczema indicating underlying atopic diathesis (atopic march). The year-round component suggests possible perennial sensitization in addition to seasonal triggers. Differential considerations include nonallergic/vasomotor rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, and acute infectious rhinitis; however, the prominence of itching, stereotypical seasonal flares, and associated eye symptoms make allergic etiology far more likely than nonallergic or infectious causes.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Skin prick testing or serum-specific IgE (sIgE) testing to confirm sensitization and identify relevant aeroallergens.
Conclusion: Allergic rhinitis with allergic conjunctivitis, exhibiting perennial symptoms with seasonal (spring) exacerbation, in an atopic patient with prior infantile eczema.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: 1) Start daily intranasal corticosteroid spray as first-line therapy for persistent nasal symptoms. 2) Add a second-generation oral antihistamine or intranasal antihistamine for control of sneezing, rhinorrhea, and pruritus. 3) Use topical anti-allergic ophthalmic drops (antihistamine/mast-cell stabilizer) during spring to address eye itching, redness, and tearing. 4) Undergo skin prick or serum-specific IgE testing to identify specific aeroallergen triggers (e.g., tree/grass pollens, dust mites, molds, animal danders) and guide avoidance. 5) Implement avoidance measures: monitor pollen counts, keep windows closed during high counts, consider high-efficiency particulate air filtration, and perform saline nasal irrigation. 6) Given the history of infantile eczema, counsel regarding the atopic predisposition and advise reporting any lower respiratory symptoms such as wheezing or chest tightness. 7) If symptoms remain inadequately controlled after 2–4 weeks of correct use or if disease modification is desired, discuss referral for allergen immunotherapy evaluation.
Notes: The prior infantile eczema confirms a background of atopy but does not change the immediate upper-airway management.

Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. criterion:

The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.

criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 30-year-old woman presents in January with 2-day history of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness. She was in her usual state of health before an abrupt onset of these symptoms. A few viral illnesses have affected her during the current winter, but not to this severity. She reports sick contacts at work and did not receive the seasonal influenza vaccine this season.
winner_protocol:
Age: 30-year-old  
Sex: Woman  
Complaint: 2-day history of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness.  
Analysis: The abrupt onset of fever, cough, headache, and generalized weakness during winter, combined with sick contacts at work and no seasonal influenza vaccination, is highly consistent with an acute viral respiratory infection such as influenza. Seasonal epidemiology and exposure history strongly support this. The main differential diagnoses include influenza, COVID-19, other respiratory viruses (e.g., RSV, rhinovirus), and less likely bacterial pneumonia or acute sinusitis. There are no described red-flag symptoms of severe disease or sepsis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Pulse oximetry, rapid influenza antigen/PCR testing, SARS-CoV-2 antigen/PCR testing.  
Conclusion: Acute febrile viral respiratory illness, most consistent with influenza, requiring outpatient evaluation and viral testing.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  
Recommendations: Obtain influenza and COVID-19 testing. Provide supportive care including antipyretics, adequate hydration, and rest. If influenza is confirmed or strongly suspected, consider initiating antiviral therapy (e.g., oseltamivir) within 48 hours of symptom onset. Practice respiratory hygiene and limit contact with others. Advise immediate return for red-flag symptoms such as shortness of breath, chest pain, confusion, or persistent high fever. Schedule follow-up if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 3–5 days. Receive the seasonal influenza vaccine once recovered.  
Notes: Pregnancy status and underlying comorbidities are not specified; these would modify risk stratification and the threshold for antiviral therapy.

Vignette: A 38-year-old male computer programmer presents with perianal discomfort and a small palpable lump that he noticed 3 days ago. He reports mild itching in the area, particularly after prolonged sitting. He denies rectal bleeding, pain during bowel movements, fever, or changes in bowel habits. He spends 8 to 10 hours daily seated at his desk. He has no family history of colorectal cancer. On examination, a small non-tender, soft, external perianal skin tag approximately 5 mm is noted at the 6 o'clock position. There is no thrombosis, bleeding, prolapse, or surrounding erythema.

Vignette:
A 38-year-old male computer programmer presents with perianal discomfort and a small palpable lump that he noticed 3 days ago. He reports mild itching in the area, particularly after prolonged sitting. He denies rectal bleeding, pain during bowel movements, fever, or changes in bowel habits. He spends 8 to 10 hours daily seated at his desk. He has no family history of colorectal cancer. On examination, a small non-tender, soft, external perianal skin tag approximately 5 mm is noted at the 6 o'clock position. There is no thrombosis, bleeding, prolapse, or surrounding erythema.
winner_protocol:
Age: 38
Sex: Male
Complaint: Perianal discomfort, small palpable lump noticed 3 days ago, and mild itching after prolonged sitting.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with a benign external perianal skin tag (fibrous tag) or a small, uncomplicated external hemorrhoid. The strongest supporting facts are the soft, non-tender, 5 mm external lesion at the 6 o'clock position without thrombosis, bleeding, prolapse, or surrounding erythema, combined with the absence of red-flag symptoms such as rectal bleeding, pain with defecation, fever, or changes in bowel habits. The patient’s prolonged sitting likely contributes to local irritation and itching. Relevant differential considerations include a residual skin tag from a prior thrombosed external hemorrhoid, a fibroepithelial polyp, and—less likely given the smooth, non-verrucous appearance—condyloma acuminata. An acute thrombosed hemorrhoid, perianal abscess, and anal fissure are effectively ruled out by the lack of tenderness, erythema, fever, and pain.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Benign external perianal skin tag without acute thrombosis, infection, or other complications.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Reassure the patient regarding the benign nature of the lesion. Advise lifestyle modifications to reduce local irritation: take standing breaks every 30–60 minutes during prolonged sitting, maintain adequate hydration, and consume a high-fiber diet to keep stools soft. Recommend gentle perianal hygiene and avoidance of harsh wiping. Warm sitz baths may be used for symptomatic itching. Refer electively to General Surgery for excision only if the tag becomes symptomatic (e.g., bleeding, significant discomfort, hygiene difficulties) or for cosmetic concerns. No colonoscopy or invasive testing is indicated at this time given the patient’s age, lack of family history of colorectal cancer, and absence of alarm features.
Notes: Return for re-evaluation if pain, bleeding, rapid growth, or new perianal lumps develop.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

The head CT has been performed, but its specific result is not described in the provided text. The punctate red spots on the right lower leg and the tongue wound are likely related to the seizure event.

winner_protocol:
Age: 16-year-old
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive right ear pain, itching, fullness, and mild hearing reduction for 4 days after daily swimming training.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for acute diffuse otitis externa (swimmer’s ear). The strongest supporting facts are: (1) recent prolonged water exposure from daily competitive swimming; (2) pain markedly worsened by tragus manipulation and auricular traction, which is characteristic of external canal inflammation rather than middle ear disease; (3) otoscopic findings of a narrowed, edematous external auditory canal with erythematous, macerated skin and scant white debris; (4) an intact tympanic membrane with no evidence of acute otitis media; and (5) absence of fever, upper respiratory symptoms, ear discharge, mastoid tenderness, lymphadenopathy, or facial nerve dysfunction. The main differential is acute otitis media, but the lack of systemic symptoms and the presence of canal skin changes with tragal tenderness make otitis externa the clear diagnosis. Sex: Female
Complaint: Dull, bilateral, band-like headache rated 4/10 beginning in the late afternoon after prolonged computer work and meetings, with mild bilateral temporal and occipital muscle tenderness on palpation.

Supporting features include the bilateral, pressing, “band-like” quality; mild intensity (4/10); absence of nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, aura, or visual changes; normal neurological and fundoscopic examinations; and pericranial muscle tenderness. The association with a stressful workday and sustained computer use is consistent with common TTH triggers. The differential includes migraine without aura, which is less likely given the lack of unilateral throbbing pain, sensory sensitivities, and autonomic symptoms. Secondary headache etiologies (e.g., intracranial mass, meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage) are effectively excluded by the chronic episodic course over one year, completely normal neurological examination, unremarkable fundoscopy, and absence of red flags such as thunderclap onset, fever, neck stiffness, or focal deficits.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: Episodic tension-type headache in a young adult with normal neurological examination and no red flags.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Reassure the patient that this is a benign primary headache disorder. For acute episodes, use over-the-counter analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen or an NSAID) as needed; limit use to fewer than 15 days per month to avoid medication-overuse headache. Implement non-pharmacological measures: regular breaks from screen work, ergonomic workstation assessment, neck and shoulder stretching, heat application to tense muscles, relaxation or biofeedback techniques, adequate hydration, and consistent sleep hygiene. Consider physical therapy or massage for pericranial muscle tenderness. Maintain a headache diary to identify triggers and monitor frequency. If headaches become more frequent, disabling, or refractory to conservative measures, consider prophylactic therapy (e.g., low-dose amitriptyline) and/or neurological follow-up. Seek urgent care immediately if red flags develop (e.g., thunderclap onset, focal neurological deficits, confusion, fever with neck stiffness, or new onset after age 50).

Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.

The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,

Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.
